summary: Describes a way to verify SSH host keys using DNS secured by DNSSEC. It defines a DNS resource record that holds a standard SSH key fingerprint, so a client can check the fingerprint it sees against the one published for the server.

eli5.summary: When you visit a server for the first time, you want to know it is the real one. This memo lets the server publish a fingerprint in the internet's phone book so you can compare.

questions: verify ssh host key with dns
how does ssh use dns to verify host keys
what is the sshfp rr type code
subtitle: Publish a fingerprint of an SSH server's key in DNS, signed with DNSSEC, so clients can check it instead of trusting blindly.

tldr.problem: When an SSH client meets a server key it has never seen, it shows a fingerprint and asks the user to accept it, and many users accept without checking.
tldr.mechanism: The server's key fingerprint is published in a new DNS record type, SSHFP (type code 44), and the client compares the key it receives with the record, trusting it only if DNSSEC authenticated the answer.
tldr.outcome: Clients get an out-of-band check on first contact, and administrators can distribute or revoke host keys by changing DNS. The check is only as strong as the DNS and DNSSEC setup behind it.

today: RFC 4255 is a Proposed Standard from January 2006, and the metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: The First-Connection Problem
sections.content:
An SSH client that connects to a server whose public key it does not know shows the user a fingerprint of the key. If the user accepts it, the key is saved locally and used to check every later connection. The RFC notes that some security-conscious users verify the fingerprint out-of-band, but many users blindly accept the key.

This document offers the out-of-band check: look up a fingerprint of the server's public key in the DNS and use DNSSEC to verify the lookup. To carry the fingerprint it defines a new DNS resource record, SSHFP. The text assumes you already understand DNS and the DNS security extensions.
sections.eli5: The first time you meet someone online, you only have their word that they are who they say. Many people just say yes without checking. This memo gives you a safe way to check.

sections.title: Verifying a Host Key with SSHFP
sections.content:
On connecting, the SSH client may look up the SSHFP records for the host. If the algorithm and fingerprint of the key the server presented match one of the returned records, the client may accept the identity of the server.

Matching has two parts. The public key algorithm and the SSHFP algorithm number MUST match, and a message digest of the public key, computed with the algorithm named by the SSHFP fingerprint type, MUST match the SSHFP fingerprint.

Client implementors SHOULD provide a configurable policy for the order of verification methods. DNS storage is one method, and local key files (from the SSH Architecture, RFC 4251) are another. If clients connect with names that are not fully qualified, the implementation SHOULD check the host key against a local database before using DNS. This helps stop an attacker who injects a DNS search path into the local resolver to push the client toward a different host.
sections.eli5: The client asks the phone book what the server's fingerprint should be. If the fingerprint on the server's key is the same as the one in the phone book, it is a match. You can also decide which to check first, your own notes or the phone book.

sections.title: Trusting the DNS Answer
sections.content:
A key verified this way MUST NOT be trusted if the SSHFP record was not authenticated by a trusted SIG record. A client that validates DNSSEC signatures itself SHOULD use standard DNSSEC validation procedures.

A client that does not validate signatures itself MUST use a secure transport between itself and whatever does the validation. The RFC gives TSIG, SIG(0) and IPsec as examples.

Without this step, the fingerprint in DNS would be just as easy to forge as the key it is meant to check.
sections.eli5: A note in the phone book only helps if it has an unbroken seal. If the seal is missing or broken, the client must not believe the note.

sections.title: The SSHFP Record
sections.content:
The SSHFP resource record stores a fingerprint of an SSH public host key tied to a DNS name. Its RR type code is 44.

The data part holds three things: an algorithm number (one octet), a fingerprint type (one octet) and the fingerprint itself. The algorithm number says which kind of public key it is: 0 is reserved, 1 is RSA and 2 is DSS. The fingerprint type names the message digest used: 0 is reserved and 1 is SHA-1.

The fingerprint is calculated over the public key blob as described in the SSH Transport Layer Protocol (RFC 4253). The digest output is placed as-is in the record. Reserving further values requires IETF consensus, and the RFC advises reserving as few fingerprint types as possible for interoperability, and only to increase security.

In text form, the record is the two numbers followed by the fingerprint in hex. Mnemonics instead of numbers are not allowed.
sections.eli5: The record is a small card with three things on it: what kind of lock the server uses, how the fingerprint was made, and the fingerprint itself written in numbers and letters.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
If a user accepts a key without checking the fingerprint through a secured channel, the connection is open to a man-in-the-middle attack. SSHFP improves this, but its overall security depends on the policies of the SSH host administrator and the DNS zone administrator, on how verification is done in the client, and on the client's diligence in using DNS securely.

Order matters. If SSHFP is checked first, new host keys can be distributed by replacing the SSHFP in DNS. If verification can be configured to require SSHFP, host key revocation can be done by removing the record from DNS.

DNSSEC only protects the fingerprint after the zone administrator signs it. So the fingerprint must reach the zone administrator securely, either by hand between the administrators or through secure DNS dynamic update between the SSH server and the name server. The RFC compares this to sending a certificate request to a certificate authority.

A different fix for the search-path problem is a trusted DNS search path, one not acquired through DHCP or other autoconfiguration. The RFC notes that current lookup APIs cannot tell whether a search path is trustworthy, so the whole client system would have to be configured that way.
sections.eli5: The phone book is only as honest as the people who write in it and the way the note gets to them. The seal protects the note once it is in the book, but someone must still hand it over safely.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA allocated RR type code 44 for SSHFP from the standard RR type space. It also opened two new registries for the SSHFP record: one for public key algorithms (0 reserved, 1 RSA, 2 DSA) and one for fingerprint types (0 reserved, 1 SHA-1). Adding new reservations to either requires IETF consensus.
sections.eli5: The keepers of the internet's lists gave this new kind of note its own number, 44, and started two small lists of allowed key kinds and fingerprint recipes.

fields.name: Algorithm
fields.desc: Public key algorithm: 1 is RSA, 2 is DSS.

fields.name: Fingerprint (variable)
fields.desc: Digest of the public key blob, placed as-is; length depends on the digest.
